subject: chemistry
title: CHM1022 summary and memory tips
summary: A condensed revision sheet for all of CHM1022: organic naming and stereochemistry, mechanisms, synthesis planning, carbonyl and aromatic chemistry, spectroscopy and transition metal complexes, plus memory aids.
body:
CHM1022 is the organic and inorganic half of first-year chemistry: how to draw and name carbon compounds, how and why they react, how to plan a route to a target molecule, how to prove a structure with spectra, and how transition metals form coloured, magnetic complexes. This sheet condenses every lesson into must-know facts, then collects the best memory aids. Use it after the lessons, not instead of them.

## Organic structure and naming

- **Skeletal structures**: every vertex and line end is a carbon; C–H hydrogens are implied so each carbon has four bonds; heteroatoms and the H on them are always drawn.
- **Structural isomers** differ in connectivity; **stereoisomers** have the same connectivity but a different 3D arrangement.
- **IUPAC recipe**: find the principal functional group (suffix), the longest chain containing it, number to give it the lowest locant, then name other groups as alphabetical prefixes.
- **Suffix priority**: carboxylic acid, then ester, amide, nitrile, aldehyde, ketone, alcohol, amine. Lower-priority groups become prefixes (hydroxy-, oxo-, amino-). Example: HOCH₂CH₂COOH is 3-hydroxypropanoic acid.
- Acid, aldehyde, amide and nitrile carbons are always C1 (no locant). Esters: alkyl part first, then -oate (ethyl ethanoate).
- A **stereocentre** has four different groups. **Enantiomers** are non-superimposable mirror images: identical physical properties except the direction they rotate plane-polarised light, and how they interact with other chiral molecules. A 50 : 50 mix is **racemic**. **Diastereomers** are stereoisomers that are not mirror images. n stereocentres give at most 2ⁿ stereoisomers.
- **CIP priorities**: higher atomic number first; at a tie, move outwards to the first point of difference; double bonds count as duplicated atoms.
- **R/S**: lowest priority pointing away, trace 1 → 2 → 3; clockwise is R, anticlockwise is S. If the lowest group is on a wedge, reverse the answer.
- **E/Z**: compare the higher-priority group on each alkene carbon; same side is Z, opposite sides is E.

## Reaction mechanisms

- A **curly arrow** moves an electron pair from a lone pair or bond to an atom or bond. Arrows start at electrons, never at a positive charge.
- **Nucleophiles** (Lewis bases) donate electron pairs: OH⁻, CN⁻, H₂O, NH₃, alkenes. **Electrophiles** (Lewis acids) accept them: H⁺, carbocations, the δ+ carbon of C–X or C=O.
- Good **leaving groups** are weak bases: I⁻ better than Br⁻, better than Cl⁻, far better than F⁻; water (from a protonated alcohol) is good, OH⁻ is poor.
- **Carbocation stability**: 3° more than 2°, more than 1°, more than methyl (hyperconjugation and inductive donation).

| | SN2 | SN1 | E2 | E1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steps | one, concerted | two, via carbocation | one, concerted | two, via carbocation |
| Rate law | k[RX][Nu] | k[RX] | k[RX][base] | k[RX] |
| Best substrate | methyl, 1° | 3° | 2°, 3° | 3° |
| Reagent | strong Nu | weak Nu | strong (bulky) base | weak base |
| Solvent | polar aprotic | polar protic | — | polar protic |
| Stereo | inversion | racemisation | anti-periplanar H and LG | — |

- Higher temperature favours elimination (more product molecules, so a more positive ΔS). **Zaitsev's rule**: the more substituted alkene is usually major.
- **Electrophilic addition to alkenes** goes via the more stable carbocation, which gives **Markovnikov's rule** (H adds to the carbon already bearing more H). Br₂ adds anti via a bromonium ion.
- **Nucleophilic addition to C=O**: Nu attacks carbon, π electrons go to O, giving an alkoxide that is then protonated.

## Planning a synthesis

- **Retrosynthesis** works backwards from the **target** using **disconnections** (⇒, "could be made from"). Each disconnection gives **synthons**, which are matched to real reagents (**synthetic equivalents**): an R⁻ synthon is a Grignard reagent, RMgBr.
- Disconnect bonds next to functional groups and near the middle of the molecule.
- Key **FGIs**: alkene + H₂O/H₃PO₄ gives an alcohol; alcohol + conc. H₂SO₄, heat gives an alkene; RX + NaOH(aq) gives an alcohol; RX + KCN gives a nitrile (+1 C); RX + excess NH₃ gives an amine; 1° alcohol + PCC gives an aldehyde; 1° alcohol + K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺, reflux gives an acid; 2° alcohol gives a ketone; 3° alcohols do not oxidise; NaBH₄ reduces aldehydes and ketones only; LiAlH₄ also reduces esters, acids and nitriles; nitrile + H₃O⁺, heat gives an acid.
- **C–C bond formation**: cyanide on a haloalkane; Grignard + methanal gives a 1° alcohol, + other aldehyde gives 2°, + ketone gives 3°, + CO₂ gives an acid (Grignards need dry conditions and no O–H or N–H in the molecule); HCN + carbonyl gives a cyanohydrin.
- **Chemoselectivity**: pick a reagent that attacks only one group (NaBH₄ reduces a ketone but not an ester). Otherwise use a **protecting group**: acetals protect C=O (removed by aqueous acid); silyl ethers protect OH (removed by fluoride).
- **Overall yield** of a linear route = product of step yields as decimals (six steps at 90% give 53%). Convergent routes and fewer steps give better yields. **Atom economy** = mass of desired product ÷ total mass of reactants × 100%.

## Carbonyl compounds

- The C=O carbon is sp², planar and δ+; nucleophiles attack it from either face (racemic product if a new stereocentre forms).
- **Aldehydes and ketones** (no leaving group) undergo **nucleophilic addition**: hydride gives alcohols, Grignards give alcohols with a new C–C bond, HCN gives cyanohydrins, alcohols give hemiacetals and acetals, 1° amines give imines. Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones (less steric crowding, less electron donation to the δ+ carbon).
- **Acid derivatives** undergo **nucleophilic acyl substitution** by **addition–elimination** through a tetrahedral intermediate (not SN2).
- **Reactivity**: acid chloride, then anhydride, then ester (and acid), then amide, most to least. Reasons: leaving-group basicity (Cl⁻ is a very weak base) and lone-pair donation into C=O (nitrogen donates most). You can go "downhill" to a less reactive derivative but not straight uphill.
- **Fischer esterification** is reversible (acid catalyst, heat; use excess alcohol or remove water). **Saponification** (ester + OH⁻) is irreversible because the carboxylate is not attacked.
- Esters react twice with Grignards (giving 3° alcohols) and with LiAlH₄ (giving 1° alcohols).
- Carboxylic acids (pKa about 4–5) are far more acidic than alcohols (about 16) because the carboxylate is resonance stabilised over two oxygens.
- **α-Hydrogens** (pKa about 19–20 for ketones) are acidic because the **enolate** is resonance stabilised. Enolates are carbon nucleophiles (α-alkylation, aldol). **Keto–enol tautomers** interconvert; the keto form is favoured.

## Aromatic compounds

- Benzene: planar, six sp² carbons, six delocalised π electrons, all C–C bonds equal (about 139 pm). Resonance energy about 150 kJ mol⁻¹ (expected 3 × 120 = 360 kJ mol⁻¹ on hydrogenation; measured about 208).
- **Aromatic** = cyclic + planar + fully conjugated + **4n + 2 π electrons** (Hückel's rule: 2, 6, 10 …). 4n π electrons in such a ring is **antiaromatic**. Aromatic: benzene, C₅H₅⁻, pyridine, pyrrole. Cyclooctatetraene puckers and is non-aromatic.
- **EAS mechanism**: make E⁺; ring attacks E⁺ to give the **arenium ion** (σ-complex; slow step, aromaticity lost); base removes H⁺ to restore aromaticity. Substitution, not addition.
- **Nitration**: conc. HNO₃/conc. H₂SO₄ makes NO₂⁺. **Halogenation**: X₂ with FeX₃ or AlCl₃. **Friedel–Crafts alkylation**: RCl/AlCl₃, but carbocations rearrange and polyalkylation occurs. **Friedel–Crafts acylation**: RCOCl/AlCl₃ via the acylium ion, with no rearrangement and only one substitution. Neither works on strongly deactivated rings.
- **Substituent effects**:

| Group | Rate | Directs |
|---|---|---|
| –NH₂, –OH, –OR, –NHCOR, alkyl | activating | ortho/para |
| –F, –Cl, –Br, –I | weakly deactivating | ortho/para |
| –CHO, –COR, –COOH, –COOR, –CN, –SO₃H, –NO₂ | deactivating | meta |

- Ortho/para directors stabilise the arenium ion by placing the positive charge next to a donor group; meta directors make ortho/para attack especially bad, so meta wins. Para often beats ortho for steric reasons.

## Spectroscopy and structure determination

- **Degree of unsaturation** = (2C + 2 + N − H − X) ÷ 2, ignoring O and S. Each ring or π bond counts 1; a benzene ring counts 4.
- **Mass spectrometry**: molecular ion M⁺• gives Mᵣ; base peak = tallest. Cl gives M : M+2 about 3 : 1; Br gives about 1 : 1. Fragments: 15 (CH₃⁺), 29 (C₂H₅⁺/CHO⁺), 43 (CH₃CO⁺/C₃H₇⁺), 77 (C₆H₅⁺), 91 (C₇H₇⁺). Odd Mᵣ means an odd number of N atoms.
- **IR** (cm⁻¹): O–H alcohol 3200–3550 broad; O–H acid 2500–3300 very broad; N–H 3300–3500; C–H just below 3000 (sp³) or just above (sp²); C≡N about 2250; C=O 1680–1750 strong and sharp; C–O 1000–1300. The fingerprint region is below 1500.
- **¹H NMR** gives four things: number of signals (H environments), chemical shift δ (deshielded H near electronegative atoms appear downfield), integration (H ratio) and splitting (n + 1 rule, from neighbouring H on adjacent carbons). Key shifts: alkyl 0.9–1.5; H–C–C=O 2.0–2.7; H–C–O 3.3–4.3; alkene 4.5–6.5; aromatic 6.5–8.0; aldehyde 9.4–10; acid 10–13. O–H signals are usually broad singlets.
- Patterns: ethyl = triplet (3H) + quartet (2H); isopropyl = doublet (6H) + septet (1H); CH₃ next to C=O or O with no H neighbours = singlet.
- **¹³C NMR** (proton-decoupled): one line per carbon environment; alkyl 10–40, C–O 50–90, C=C and aromatic 110–160, acid/ester/amide C=O 160–185, aldehyde/ketone C=O 190–220.
- **Strategy**: DoU → MS → IR → ¹³C → ¹H → assemble → check every peak.

## Transition metal chemistry

- 4s fills before 3d in atoms, but **4s electrons are lost first** in cations. Cr is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹, Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. d-electron count of a first-row ion = group number − oxidation state (Co³⁺: 9 − 3 = d⁶).
- Variable oxidation states arise because 4s and 3d are close in energy (Mn reaches +7 in MnO₄⁻).
- **Ligands** are Lewis bases that donate a lone pair to the metal (a Lewis acid) through a **coordinate bond**. Monodentate (H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻, CN⁻, CO), bidentate (en, oxalate), hexadentate (EDTA⁴⁻). The **chelate effect** (extra stability of chelates) is mainly an entropy effect.
- **Coordination number** = number of donor atoms. 2 linear; 4 tetrahedral or square planar (d⁸); 6 octahedral. Cis–trans isomers exist for square planar and octahedral complexes (cisplatin); [M(en)₃] complexes are chiral.
- Metal oxidation state = overall charge − sum of ligand charges.
- **Naming**: cation before anion; ligands alphabetically, then metal; di-/tri-/tetra- (bis-/tris- for complex ligand names); anionic ligands end in -o (chlorido, cyanido); aqua, ammine, carbonyl; oxidation state in Roman numerals; anionic complexes end in -ate (ferrate, cuprate). Example: K₃[Fe(CN)₆] is potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III).
- **Crystal field theory (octahedral)**: d(z²) and d(x²−y²) point at the ligands and rise (e_g); d(xy), d(xz), d(yz) are lower (t₂g). The gap is Δₒ. Tetrahedral splitting is reversed and smaller (about 4/9 Δₒ).
- **Spectrochemical series** (weak to strong field): I⁻, Br⁻, Cl⁻, F⁻, OH⁻, H₂O, NH₃, en, CN⁻, CO.
- For d⁴–d⁷ octahedral ions: weak field (Δₒ less than pairing energy) gives **high spin**; strong field gives **low spin**. [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is high spin (4 unpaired); [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ is low spin (0 unpaired).
- **Paramagnetic** = unpaired electrons; **diamagnetic** = all paired. Spin-only moment μ = √(n(n + 2)) μ_B.
- **Colour** comes from d–d transitions: Δ = hc/λ (per photon; multiply by N_A for per mole). The colour seen is complementary to the colour absorbed. d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions (Sc³⁺, Zn²⁺) are colourless. A stronger-field ligand absorbs shorter wavelengths.

## Tips to remember

**Structure and naming**
- Suffix priority (made-up memory trick): "**A**cids **E**at **A**ll **N**ice **A**pples, **K**iwis **A**nd **A**vocados" = acid, ester, amide, nitrile, aldehyde, ketone, alcohol, amine.
- "**Z = Ze Zame Zide**": Z puts the higher-priority groups on the same side; E is "Enemies, opposite sides".
- R/S: "**Steering wheel**": point the lowest group away (like the steering column) and turn 1 → 2 → 3; turning right (clockwise) is R.
- Wedge trap: "**H on a wedge? Flip the answer.**"

**Mechanisms**
- "**SN2 is a one-step mugging from behind**": the nucleophile attacks the back as the leaving group runs out the front, flipping the molecule like an umbrella in the wind.
- "**SN1: one waits alone**": the substrate ionises on its own first, so only [RX] appears in the rate law.
- "**Tertiary can't take a backside attack**": too crowded for SN2, so 3° goes SN1/E1 or E2.
- "**Heat favours elimination**" because elimination makes more molecules (entropy).
- Markovnikov: "**The rich get richer**": H goes to the carbon that already has more H, because that leaves the more stable carbocation.

**Synthesis and carbonyls**
- "**NaBH₄ is the gentle one**" (aldehydes and ketones only); "**LiAlH₄ is the sledgehammer**" (also esters, acids, nitriles).
- Grignard alcohol class: "**methanal 1, aldehyde 2, ketone 3**" — the alcohol class matches the number of carbon groups on the C–OH carbon.
- Acid-derivative reactivity, most to least (made-up memory trick): "**Clever Ants Eat Apples**" = acid Chloride, Anhydride, Ester, Amide. You can only roll downhill.
- Yields multiply: "**every step takes its tax**" — 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 is already only 73%.

**Aromatics**
- Hückel: "**4n + 2 is good for you; 4n is a sin**" (aromatic versus antiaromatic). Benzene's 6 is the classic 4n + 2.
- "**Donors go O and P; pullers go Meta**": lone-pair donors and alkyl groups direct ortho/para; groups with a δ+ atom next to the ring (C=O, NO₂, CN) direct meta.
- Halogens are the "**odd couple**": they deactivate (pull by induction) but direct ortho/para (donate by resonance).
- "**Acylation stops, alkylation flops**": acylation gives one clean product; alkylation rearranges and over-reacts.

**Spectroscopy**
- DoU of 4 with six or more carbons: "**four means benzene, probably**".
- IR: "**1700 is the carbonyl, 3300 is the OH or NH**". Broad and very wide down to 2500 = carboxylic acid.
- n + 1 rule: "**count the neighbours, add one**". Ethyl = "**triplet-quartet couple**"; isopropyl = "**doublet of six, septet of one**".
- ¹H NMR order of information: "**How many, Where, How big, How split**" (signals, shift, integration, splitting).

**Transition metals**
- "**4s: first in, first out**".
- d count = "**group minus charge**".
- Spectrochemical series (made-up memory trick): "**I Bring Clean Fresh Old Water, No Extra Cyanide, Carbon**" = I⁻, Br⁻, Cl⁻, F⁻, OH⁻, H₂O, NH₃, en, CN⁻, CO.
- "**Strong field, low spin, paired in**"; "**weak field, high spin, spread out**".
- "**You see what is left**": a complex looks the complementary colour of the light it absorbs.

**If you remember one thing:** organic reactions are electron-rich atoms attacking electron-poor atoms. Find the nucleophile, find the electrophile, and the curly arrows (and most products) follow.

## Summary

- Name by principal group, longest chain and lowest locants; assign R/S and E/Z with CIP priorities; n stereocentres give at most 2ⁿ stereoisomers.
- Curly arrows go from nucleophile to electrophile; substrate, reagent, solvent and temperature decide between SN1, SN2, E1 and E2; alkenes follow Markovnikov.
- Plan syntheses backwards with disconnections, FGIs, C–C bond formation and protecting groups; linear yields multiply.
- Aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition; acid derivatives undergo addition–elimination in the order acid chloride, anhydride, ester, amide.
- Aromatic rings follow Hückel's 4n + 2 rule and undergo electrophilic substitution, with substituents controlling rate and position.
- Combine DoU, MS, IR and NMR to solve structures; crystal field theory explains the colour and magnetism of transition metal complexes.

questions.prompt: What is the IUPAC name of HOCH₂CH₂CHO?
questions.explanation: The aldehyde outranks the alcohol, so it takes the suffix (-al) and is C1; the OH on C3 becomes the prefix hydroxy-, giving 3-hydroxypropanal. C is the tempting wrong answer: it treats the alcohol as the principal group, but aldehydes have higher priority. A compound can only have one suffix, so D is not allowed.

questions.prompt: In one stereoisomer of 2-chlorobut-2-ene, CH₃–C(Cl)=CH–CH₃, the Cl atom and the H atom on the double bond are on the same side. How is this isomer labelled?

options.A: Z, because Cl and H are on the same side
options.B: Z, because the two CH₃ groups are on the same side
options.C: E, because the higher-priority groups are on opposite sides
options.D: Neither, because one carbon has two identical groups

questions.explanation: On C2, Cl outranks CH₃; on C3, CH₃ outranks H. If Cl and H are on the same side, then Cl and the C3 methyl (the two higher-priority groups) are on opposite sides, so the isomer is E. A is the trap: you compare the higher-priority group on each carbon, not whichever atoms you happen to look at. D is wrong because each alkene carbon carries two different groups.

questions.prompt: (R)-3-bromo-3-methylhexane, a chiral tertiary bromide, is warmed in water. Which statement about the substitution product, 3-methylhexan-3-ol, is correct?

options.A: It is formed with complete inversion of configuration
options.B: It is formed with complete retention of configuration
options.C: No substitution occurs because water is a weak nucleophile
options.D: It is formed as a mixture of both configurations, largely racemic

questions.explanation: A 3° substrate with a weak nucleophile in a protic solvent reacts by SN1. The leaving group departs first to give a planar carbocation, which water can attack from either face, so both configurations form (largely racemic). A describes SN2, which cannot occur at a crowded 3° carbon. C is wrong: weak nucleophiles are exactly what SN1 needs.

questions.prompt: Why does raising the temperature favour elimination over substitution for the same substrate and reagent?

options.A: Elimination produces more molecules, so it has a more positive ΔS and −TΔS becomes more favourable
options.B: Elimination is always exothermic and substitution is endothermic
options.C: High temperature makes nucleophiles weaker bases
options.D: Carbocations are only formed at high temperature

questions.explanation: Elimination turns two reactant species into three product species (alkene, leaving group and protonated base), so ΔS is more positive. In ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, a larger T makes the entropy term more important, favouring elimination. B is an invented generalisation; D is wrong because carbocations form in SN1 and E1 at ordinary temperatures.

questions.prompt: In a retrosynthesis, a disconnection produces the synthon CH₃CH₂⁻ (an ethyl carbanion). Which reagent is its usual synthetic equivalent?
questions.explanation: A Grignard reagent has a highly polarised C–Mg bond with carbon δ−, so it reacts as a source of the carbanion R⁻. A is the tempting choice because it contains the ethyl group, but in bromoethane the carbon is δ+ — it is the synthetic equivalent of the cation CH₃CH₂⁺, the opposite synthon.

questions.prompt: A chemist wants to convert ethyl propanoate into propan-1-ol. Which reagent should be used?

options.C: LiAlH₄ in dry ether, then H₃O⁺

questions.explanation: Esters are only reduced by the powerful hydride donor LiAlH₄, which reduces the acyl part to a 1° alcohol (here propan-1-ol, plus ethanol from the alkoxy part). A is the tempting answer, but NaBH₄ is too weak to reduce esters; it reduces only aldehydes and ketones. B and D are oxidising agents.

questions.prompt: Why are amides the least reactive carboxylic acid derivatives towards nucleophilic acyl substitution?

options.A: The C=O bond in amides is much weaker than in esters
options.B: The nitrogen lone pair delocalises into the C=O, reducing the δ+ on carbon, and NH₂⁻ is a very poor leaving group
options.C: Amides cannot form a tetrahedral intermediate
options.D: Nitrogen is more electronegative than oxygen, so it withdraws electrons from the carbonyl carbon

questions.explanation: Nitrogen is the least electronegative of the attached atoms (compared with O and Cl), so its lone pair is the best at donating into the carbonyl, making the carbon less electrophilic; and NH₂⁻ (pKa of NH₃ about 35) is a very strong base and so a terrible leaving group. D is the trap: nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, not more.

questions.prompt: How many π electrons in pyrrole (a five-membered ring with four CH groups and one NH) are counted for Hückel's rule, and is it aromatic?
questions.explanation: Pyrrole's two C=C bonds give 4 π electrons, and the nitrogen lone pair sits in a p orbital that is part of the ring's π system, adding 2: 6 = 4n + 2 with n = 1, so it is aromatic. A counts only the C=C electrons. (Contrast pyridine, whose N lone pair lies in the ring plane and is not counted.)

questions.prompt: Chlorobenzene undergoes nitration more slowly than benzene, but the products are mainly ortho and para. Why?

options.A: Chlorine withdraws electrons inductively (deactivating) but donates a lone pair by resonance, stabilising ortho/para arenium ions
options.B: Chlorine donates electrons inductively and withdraws them by resonance
options.C: Chlorine blocks the meta positions sterically
options.D: Chlorine is a meta director, but meta products rearrange to ortho and para

questions.explanation: Chlorine is electronegative, so its inductive pull lowers the electron density of the whole ring and slows the reaction. Its lone pairs can still donate into the arenium ion when attack is ortho or para, giving an extra resonance form. B reverses both effects. Halogens are the classic exception to 'deactivating means meta'.

questions.prompt: A compound C₃H₆O shows a strong, sharp IR absorption at 1715 cm⁻¹, no absorption above 3000 cm⁻¹ other than C–H, and a ¹H NMR spectrum with a single singlet. What is it?
questions.explanation: 1715 cm⁻¹ shows a C=O. Propanone's six H are all equivalent (two CH₃ groups related by symmetry, with no H neighbours), so they give one singlet. A also has C=O, but it would show three signals, including an aldehyde H near 9.8 ppm. C has an O–H and would show a broad band above 3200 cm⁻¹; D has no C=O.

questions.prompt: How many signals appear in the proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum of 1,4-dimethylbenzene?
questions.explanation: Symmetry makes the two CH₃ carbons equivalent (1 signal), the two ring carbons carrying CH₃ equivalent (1 signal) and the four ring CH carbons equivalent (1 signal): 3 signals. D counts every carbon without using symmetry. A misses that ring carbons with and without substituents are different environments.

questions.prompt: How many unpaired electrons does the high-spin octahedral complex [Mn(H₂O)₆]²⁺ have, and what is its spin-only magnetic moment?
questions.explanation: Mn²⁺ is d⁵ (group 7 − 2). Water is a weak-field ligand, so in the high-spin arrangement t₂g³ e_g² all five electrons are unpaired, and μ = √(5 × 7) = √35 = 5.92 μ_B. A is the low-spin result (t₂g⁵, one unpaired), which would need a strong-field ligand such as CN⁻.
